name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Matching root types with their plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Root Type / Structure) List-II (Feature / Example)
A. Tap root system I. Replaces primary root from stem base, as in wheat
B. Fibrous root system II. Direct elongation of radicle, as in mustard
C. Adventitious roots III. Thimble-like protective structure at root apex
D. Root cap IV. Originates from parts other than radicle, as in Monstera

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the characteristics of the tap root system
In dicotyledonous plants, the direct elongation of the embryonic radicle forms the primary root, which bears lateral branches of multiple orders, constituting the tap root system seen in mustard.

Step 2: Identify the characteristics of the fibrous root system
In monocotyledonous plants, the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by numerous roots originating from the base of the stem, forming the fibrous root system found in wheat.

Step 3: Identify the characteristics of adventitious roots
When roots develop from parts of the plant other than the embryonic radicle, such as in grass, Monstera, and banyan, they are classified as adventitious roots.

Step 4: Identify the function of the root cap
The apex of the root is covered and protected from mechanical injury during soil penetration by a thimble-like covering called the root cap.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Tap root system pairs with Direct elongation of radicle, as in mustard; Fibrous root system pairs with Replaces primary root from stem base, as in wheat; Adventitious roots pair with Originates from parts other than radicle, as in Monstera; and Root cap pairs with Thimble-like protective structure at root apex.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Matching regions of root with their functions

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Region of Root Tip) List-II (Defining Feature / Activity)
A. Root cap I. Epidermal cells form fine root hairs for absorption
B. Region of meristematic activity II. Rapid cell enlargement responsible for root growth in length
C. Region of elongation III. Thimble-like protective structure covering the tender apex
D. Region of maturation IV. Very small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide repeatedly

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate the root cap
The root cap is a protective, thimble-like structure situated at the root apex that cushions the tender apical meristem as it penetrates the soil.

Step 2: Evaluate the region of meristematic activity
Located a few millimetres above the root cap, the meristematic zone consists of very small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide continuously.

Step 3: Evaluate the region of elongation
Proximal to the meristematic zone, the cells undergo rapid elongation and enlargement, contributing directly to the linear growth of the root.

Step 4: Evaluate the region of maturation
In this zone, cells differentiate and mature; some epidermal cells produce fine, delicate, tubular thread-like root hairs that absorb water and mineral nutrients from the soil.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Root cap pairs with Thimble-like protective structure covering the tender apex; Region of meristematic activity pairs with Very small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide repeatedly; Region of elongation pairs with Rapid cell enlargement responsible for root growth in length; and Region of maturation pairs with Epidermal cells form fine root hairs for absorption.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - Matching phyllotaxy patterns with characteristic plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Leaf Pattern / Type) List-II (Plant Example)
A. Alternate phyllotaxy I. Calotropis and guava
B. Opposite phyllotaxy II. Silk cotton
C. Whorled phyllotaxy III. China rose and sunflower
D. Palmately compound leaf IV. Alstonia

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand alternate phyllotaxy
In alternate phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node in an alternating sequence along the stem or branch, as found in china rose, mustard, and sunflower.

Step 2: Understand opposite phyllotaxy
In opposite phyllotaxy, a pair of leaves arises at each node and lies directly opposite to each other, as observed in Calotropis and guava.

Step 3: Understand whorled phyllotaxy
When more than two leaves arise at a single node and form a distinct circle or whorl, it is termed whorled phyllotaxy, characteristic of Alstonia.

Step 4: Understand palmately compound leaves
In palmately compound leaves, multiple leaflets radiate outward from a common single attachment point located at the tip of the petiole, as in silk cotton.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Alternate phyllotaxy pairs with China rose and sunflower; Opposite phyllotaxy pairs with Calotropis and guava; Whorled phyllotaxy pairs with Alstonia; and Palmately compound leaf pairs with Silk cotton.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q04 - Matching types of floral symmetry with examples

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Floral Character / Symmetry) List-II (Plant Example)
A. Actinomorphic flower I. Canna
B. Zygomorphic flower II. Lily
C. Asymmetric flower III. Pea, gulmohur, and Cassia
D. Perianth present IV. Mustard, datura, and chilli

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze actinomorphic floral symmetry
A flower that displays radial symmetry, meaning it can be bisected into two identical halves along any radial plane passing through the central axis, is actinomorphic, as seen in mustard, datura, and chilli.

Step 2: Analyze zygomorphic floral symmetry
A flower exhibiting bilateral symmetry, where it can be divided into two similar halves in only one specific vertical plane, is zygomorphic, as found in pea, gulmohur, bean, and Cassia.

Step 3: Analyze asymmetric flowers
A flower is irregular or asymmetric when it cannot be divided into two similar halves along any vertical plane passing through the centre, as in Canna.

Step 4: Analyze the perianth condition
When the calyx and corolla are undifferentiated and fused or indistinguishable from each other, the whorl is designated as a perianth, typically seen in flowers of lily.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Actinomorphic flower pairs with Mustard, datura, and chilli; Zygomorphic flower pairs with Pea, gulmohur, and Cassia; Asymmetric flower pairs with Canna; and Perianth present pairs with Lily.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q05 - Matching ovary positions with representative plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Floral Type / Inflorescence) List-II (Ovary Position / Characteristic)
A. Hypogynous flower I. Thalamus completely encloses ovary, ovary is inferior (guava, cucumber)
B. Perigynous flower II. Gynoecium occupies highest position, ovary is superior (mustard, brinjal)
C. Epigynous flower III. Main axis terminates in a flower, flowers in basipetal order
D. Cymose inflorescence IV. Floral parts situated on thalamus rim at ovary level, ovary half inferior (plum, rose)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define hypogynous flowers
In hypogynous flowers, the gynoecium occupies the uppermost position on the thalamus while other floral whorls arise below it, giving rise to a superior ovary as in mustard, china rose, and brinjal.

Step 2: Define perigynous flowers
In perigynous flowers, the gynoecium is centrally positioned and the remaining floral parts arise along the elevated rim of the thalamus at essentially the same level, resulting in a half-inferior ovary as in plum, rose, and peach.

Step 3: Define epigynous flowers
In epigynous flowers, the thalamus margin grows upward to enclose the ovary entirely and fuses with its wall, so that calyx, corolla, and stamens arise above the ovary, rendering the ovary inferior as in guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower.

Step 4: Define cymose inflorescence
In cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates directly into a flower, restricting its indeterminate growth, and flowers are produced in a basipetal sequence.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Hypogynous flower pairs with Gynoecium occupies highest position, ovary is superior (mustard, brinjal); Perigynous flower pairs with Floral parts situated on thalamus rim at ovary level, ovary half inferior (plum, rose); Epigynous flower pairs with Thalamus completely encloses ovary, ovary is inferior (guava, cucumber); and Cymose inflorescence pairs with Main axis terminates in a flower, flowers in basipetal order.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q06 - Matching corolla aestivation types with plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of Aestivation) List-II (Arrangement and Example)
A. Valvate I. Margins overlap one another but not in any particular direction, as in Cassia
B. Twisted II. Standard petal overlaps two wings which overlap two keels, as in pea
C. Imbricate III. Margins touch one another without overlapping, as in Calotropis
D. Vexillary IV. One margin overlaps that of the adjacent member regularly, as in cotton

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine valvate aestivation
In valvate aestivation, sepals or petals within a whorl merely touch each other along their adjacent margins without any overlapping, as seen in Calotropis.

Step 2: Examine twisted aestivation
In twisted aestivation, one margin of each petal or sepal systematically overlaps that of the next consecutive member in a uniform direction, as in china rose, lady's finger, and cotton.

Step 3: Examine imbricate aestivation
In imbricate aestivation, the margins of the appendages overlap irregularly rather than in any single consistent direction, as observed in Cassia and gulmohur.

Step 4: Examine vexillary aestivation
In vexillary or papilionaceous aestivation, five distinct petals exist: the largest posterior petal (standard) overlaps two lateral petals (wings), which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior fused petals (keel), as seen in pea and bean.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Valvate pairs with Margins touch one another without overlapping, as in Calotropis; Twisted pairs with One margin overlaps that of the adjacent member regularly, as in cotton; Imbricate pairs with Margins overlap one another but not in any particular direction, as in Cassia; and Vexillary pairs with Standard petal overlaps two wings which overlap two keels, as in pea.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Matching stamen fusion and cohesion with examples

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Condition of Stamens) List-II (Defining Feature / Example)
A. Epipetalous I. Stamens attached to perianth, as in lily
B. Epiphyllous II. Stamens united into a single bundle, as in china rose
C. Monoadelphous III. Stamens united into two bundles, as in pea
D. Diadelphous IV. Stamens attached to petals, as in brinjal

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the epipetalous condition
When stamens are physically fused or attached by their filaments to the petals of the corolla, they are described as epipetalous, as seen in brinjal.

Step 2: Understand the epiphyllous condition
When stamens are attached directly to the perianth segments (tepals), they are termed epiphyllous, as observed in flowers of lily.

Step 3: Understand monoadelphous cohesion
When the filaments of all stamens in a flower are united together into a single continuous bundle or tube, the condition is termed monoadelphous, as in china rose.

Step 4: Understand diadelphous cohesion
When stamens are united into two distinct clusters or bundles, the condition is termed diadelphous, as classically seen in pea.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Epipetalous pairs with Stamens attached to petals, as in brinjal; Epiphyllous pairs with Stamens attached to perianth, as in lily; Monoadelphous pairs with Stamens united into a single bundle, as in china rose; and Diadelphous pairs with Stamens united into two bundles, as in pea.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Matching placentation types with their representative examples

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Placentation Type) List-II (Structural Description and Example)
A. Marginal I. Ovules borne on central axis without any septa, as in Dianthus
B. Axile II. Placenta forms a ridge along ventral suture bearing two rows of ovules, as in pea
C. Parietal III. Placenta is axial in a multilocular ovary, as in lemon and tomato
D. Free central IV. Ovules develop on inner ovary wall with a false septum, as in mustard

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify marginal placentation
In marginal placentation, the placenta forms an elongated ridge along the ventral suture of a monocarpellary ovary, bearing ovules in two parallel rows, as seen in pea.

Step 2: Identify axile placentation
In axile placentation, the ovary is multilocular and the placentae develop along the central axis where septa meet, bearing ovules in each locule, as in china rose, tomato, and lemon.

Step 3: Identify parietal placentation
In parietal placentation, ovules develop directly on the inner wall or periphery of a unilocular ovary, which may become two-chambered due to a false septum (replum), as in mustard and Argemone.

Step 4: Identify free central placentation
In free central placentation, ovules develop on a free central column within an unilocular ovary that completely lacks partitioning septa, as in Dianthus and primrose.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Marginal pairs with Placenta forms a ridge along ventral suture bearing two rows of ovules, as in pea; Axile pairs with Placenta is axial in a multilocular ovary, as in lemon and tomato; Parietal pairs with Ovules develop on inner ovary wall with a false septum, as in mustard; and Free central pairs with Ovules borne on central axis without any septa, as in Dianthus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Matching parts of monocot seed with descriptions

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Seed Part / Structure) List-II (Anatomical Identity / Function)
A. Aleurone layer I. Protective sheath enclosing the embryonic plumule
B. Scutellum II. Protective sheath enclosing the embryonic radicle
C. Coleoptile III. Proteinous outer layer separating embryo from endosperm
D. Coleorhiza IV. Large, shield-shaped single cotyledon of grass embryo

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the aleurone layer
In monocotyledonous seeds such as maize, the bulky food-storing endosperm is delimited externally from the embryo by a specialized proteinous envelope called the aleurone layer.

Step 2: Understand the scutellum
The embryo of a monocotyledonous seed occupies a groove at one end of the endosperm and possesses a single, large, shield-shaped cotyledon termed the scutellum.

Step 3: Understand the coleoptile
The embryonal axis bears a shoot apex (plumule) and embryonic leaf primordia that are completely enclosed within a protective tubular foliar sheath known as the coleoptile.

Step 4: Understand the coleorhiza
At the lower end of the embryonal axis, the embryonic root (radicle) and its protective root cap are encased within an undifferentiated protective sheath designated as the coleorhiza.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Aleurone layer pairs with Proteinous outer layer separating embryo from endosperm; Scutellum pairs with Large, shield-shaped single cotyledon of grass embryo; Coleoptile pairs with Protective sheath enclosing the embryonic plumule; and Coleorhiza pairs with Protective sheath enclosing the embryonic radicle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q10 - Matching floral organs of Solanaceae with features

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Whorl of Solanaceae) List-II (Morphological Characteristic)
A. Calyx I. Petals five, united, showing valvate aestivation
B. Corolla II. Stamens five, epipetalous, alternipetalous
C. Androecium III. Bicarpellary syncarpous, superior ovary with swollen placenta
D. Gynoecium IV. Sepals five, united, persistent with valvate aestivation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Characterize the calyx of Solanaceae
The calyx in Solanaceae possesses five united sepals (gamosepalous) with valvate aestivation, and it characteristically remains persistent in the fruiting stage (as seen in brinjal and tomato).

Step 2: Characterize the corolla of Solanaceae
The corolla consists of five united petals (gamopetalous) with valvate aestivation, exhibiting shapes such as tubular, funnel-shaped, or rotate.

Step 3: Characterize the androecium of Solanaceae
The androecium is composed of five distinct stamens that are epipetalous (filaments attached to the corolla tube).

Step 4: Characterize the gynoecium of Solanaceae
The gynoecium is bicarpellary and syncarpous, with an obliquely placed superior bilocular ovary containing numerous ovules arranged on a prominent, swollen axile placenta.

Step 5: Final conclusion
The correct pairings are: Calyx pairs with Sepals five, united, persistent with valvate aestivation; Corolla pairs with Petals five, united, showing valvate aestivation; Androecium pairs with Stamens five, epipetalous, alternipetalous; and Gynoecium pairs with Bicarpellary syncarpous, superior ovary with swollen placenta.
